TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS = 3600

    def __init__(self, users: dict[str, User], mailer: Mailer, clock: Clock) -> None:
        self.users = users
        self.mailer = mailer
        self.clock = clock
        self._resets: dict[str, tuple[str, float]] = {}

    def request_reset(self, email: str) -> None:
        if email not in self.users:
            # Don't reveal whether an email is registered.
            return

        token = new_token()
        expires_at = self.clock.now() + self.TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS
        self._resets[token] = (email, expires_at)

        link = RESET_LINK_TEMPLATE.format(token=token)
        self.mailer.send(
            to=email,
            subject="Reset your password",
            body=f"Click the link below to reset your password:\n\n{link}\n\n"
            "If you didn't request this, you can ignore this email.",
        )

    def reset_password(self, token: str, new_password: str) -> bool:
        entry = self._resets.get(token)
        if entry is None:
            return False

        email, expires_at = entry
        # Single-use: remove the token whether or not it's still valid.
        del self._resets[token]

        if self.clock.now() > expires_at:
            return False

        user = self.users.get(email)
        if user is None:
            return False

        user.password_hash = hash_password(new_password)
        return True

All 3 tests pass. Implementation summary:

- `request_reset(email)`: silently no-ops for unknown emails (avoids leaking account existence), otherwise generates a token via `new_token()`, stores it with an expiry (`clock.now() + TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`), and emails a link built with `RESET_LINK_TEMPLATE`.
- `reset_password(token, new_password)`: looks up the token, deletes it immediately (single-use), and returns `False` for unknown/expired tokens or missing users; otherwise updates `password_hash` via `hash_password` and returns `True`.
- All time checks go through the injected `Clock`, never `time.time()`.
